Hello, my name is Lasse Rempe, and I am Professor of Pure Mathematics at the University of Manchester. I work in complex analysis and particularly complex dynamics.

I have been somewhat interested in formalisation for at least 20 years, but had not done much myself, except proposing a little formalisation challenge about Misiurewicz's theorem on the FOM mailing list some years ago, which John Harrison quickly solved in HOL Light.

I have been interested in and somewhat lurking on Lean also for quite some years, since I had some discussions with Kevin Buzzard, but I only did my first formalisation with the help of AI a couple of weeks ago, when I obtained a Lean formalisation of Misiurewicz's theorem mentioned above and some related statements:
https://palomar-registry.org/entry?id=PALOMAR-2026-09-16-000001&version=1

I have since done some further auto-formalisation work such as this, which is waiting to appear on Palomar:
https://github.com/LR-UK/Bounded-orbit-wandering-domains/

I would be very interested in collaborating to getting more of the foundational material in complex analysis and complex dynamics into a shared library, whether that be in Mathlib or in a more permissive library that also allows for AI-generated proofs. (I think a real issue lies in making sure that the STATEMENTS and DEFINITIONS are correct, though.) We seem to be entering a Wild West era where everyone can do their formalisations from scratch using AI tools, and it would be really good to have a unified library at least of the fundamental concepts and results in the field.

I hope to find some like-minded people in the field on this Zulip. I also have a group of junior colleagues with whom we are trying to get involved in Lean formalisation, and whom I have encouraged to sign up to Zulip themselves.

One of our goals is to identify a small topic that it would be worthwhile to bring forward to inclusion in Mathlib, but this would help having some advice from those who are familiar with the processes, and what is currently on Mathlib in terms of complex analysis.
Welcome!
Welcome! I very much agree that there's a big complex-analysis-shaped gap in Mathlib's coverage. I would love to hear more about your plans!

Welcome! As a student of Dierk Schleicher in a previous life, I'm very excited to see more complex analysis and holomorphic dynamics in mathlib. In general, mathlib (intentionally) has very high standards on code --- think of it like a new version of Bourbaki: statements should be appropriately general, code of high quality, etc. Vanilla AI-written code usually doesn't cut it, but we're happy to teach interested users about mathlib's ways and help them polish their contribution. In my experience as mathlib maintainer, this only works if you as the author are willing to learn some Lean yourself.

For AI-generated code, the Tau Ceti library is a better home: while having slightly lower standards, it aims to centralise all the AI-generated code in a shared library building on top of mathlib. If you're more interested in letting the AI do the work for you, that's a better place. My opinion is that in the long run, getting things to mathlib-level is very desirable, but getting it into Tau Ceti is much better than it staying in a personal repository where it's being re-invented all the time.

Hello Michael! Yes, we are interested in contributing to Mathlib, but also in contributing results with checked statements & thought-through definitions, but AI-generated proofs. I thought that Tau Ceti might be a good home for this, do you have advice on how to contribute there? For example, I have an AI-generated formalisation of Runge's theorem, which I don't think currently is on Tau Ceti.

It sounds like it's roadmap time :map:

https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCetiRoadmap/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md

Lasse Rempe said:

what is currently on Mathlib in terms of complex analysis

Here's a list I keep of well-known theorems that are missing, to the best of my knowledge

Complex analysis theorems

  • Borel-Carathéodory theorem
  • Casorati-Weierstrass theorem
  • Cauchy integral formula
  • Cauchy integral theorem
  • Cauchy residue theorem
  • Cauchy-Riemann equations
  • Cauchy's argument principle
  • Hurwitz's theorem
  • Identity theorem
  • Liouville's theorem
  • Maximum modulus principle
  • Minimum modulus principle
  • Montel's theorem
  • Morera's theorem
  • Open mapping theorem
  • Phragmén-Lindelöf principle
  • Picard's great theorem
  • Picard's little theorem
  • Riemann mapping theorem (#33505 but possibly abandoned, Tau Ceti roadmap)
  • Rouché's theorem
  • Schwarz lemma
  • Schwarz reflection principle
  • Schwarz-Pick theorem
  • Weierstrass factorization theorem
@Chris Birkbeck has a lot of expertise with upstreaming projects to Tau Ceti.

Yes so the best thing to do as a start would be to ask your agent to look at the roadmaps in tau ceti and this and then suggest roadmaps that we may want in tau ceti. I then look over the suggestions and work with the AI to produce roadmaps that contain things that one would consider reusable or of general interest for your area. The idea of a roadmap is that it should outline a path from where tau ceti is right now to where you want it to be (for example to include the reusable parts of the formalisation projects you have already done). For this I find a combination of a human listing basic things a roadmap on a particular area should have, together with an AI checking for errors or gaps and finding out what tau ceti already has in other roadmas, quickly converges on a good roadmap.
Feel free to make some draft PRs with roadmaps and I (or more likely my AI) can have a look and give you feedback
As people have said, we need more complex analysis, so this would be very welcome indeed!

Hi Lasse! As you are already well aware, there are several games you can play here:

1) you can try and get stuff into mathlib;
2) you can make your own repo and put stuff in that.
3) you can try and get stuff into an AI library like Tau Ceti;

The most natural thing to do before you start anything is to choose a target or several related targets, perhaps from Snir's list above. Then you have to choose how to get them done. What is the point of doing them? Is it to teach yourself Lean? To teach your junior colleagues Lean? To learn no Lean at all but to marvel as AI formalizes everything for you? There are many different ways to play the game right now.

1) mathlib. Writing code for mathlib is like contributing to Bourbaki. Every line gets scrutinised. You don't make a definition for C\mathbb{C}C if the same definition works for a complex vector space or a complex manifold or a complete nontrivially-normed field or whatever -- you make the definition in the correct generality. This is all about learning to think in the right abstraction and mathlib holds these things very dear. I strongly believe that it was these principles that got mathlib this far. It is not everyone's cup of tea but it can be very satisfying to do mathematics in this way. The learning curve is brutal. AI slop is unlikely to be tolerated. You contribute slowly at first, and you will need to ask lots of questions here -- and you will quickly get helpful answers the moment people realise that you or your group are attempting to learn how to become good Lean coders. Mathlib is like artisanal formalization and it is how many of us here began our journey.

But now there are other ways to play.
2) Your own repo. You can make your own repo, choose something which you want to do, figure out how to state it (e.g. by asking for help) and then figure out how to prove it, either by reading books like #mil or just by asking AI and then not bothering to understand the answer and just checking that it compiles. A lot depends on whether you want to really learn how to use the software or just see it working in practice.

3) Tau Ceti. And then finally, as has already been pointed out, you can instead decide that you would like to see an area formalized and you can write a "roadmap" for how to do it (similar to designing a study group), which is an English text describing what needs to be done. You then give it to a machine and the machine does it and you don't need to do anything else at all, you can watch it or ignore it. In the end it is added to Tau Ceti. This is probably the quickest way to get a theorem formalized and of course it's also the way that you learn the least about Lean because for this route you don't have to write even one line of Lean code.

So -- what do you actually want to do?

Thanks @Snir Broshi @Chris Birkbeck @Kevin Buzzard ! I guess the answer to what I wanted to do is a bit of several things - I'd like us to contribute to Mathlib. But my main goal is to have a good shared repository for the field, with the right definitions and statements. I'm less bothered about the proofs for the moment, as long as they compile, but there's an argument not to create too much bloat also. So if I already have a formalisation, can it be added to Tau Ceti if it compiles and the statements are agreed?

The good shared repository for the field with the right definitions and statements is arguably mathlib -- this is one of the reasons it exists.

If you already have a formalisation then yes, it can be added to Tau Ceti; indeed the UEA group is very fond of doing things this way; slop it out and then write the roadmap afterwards and get the agents to look at the slop and make it better.
Fair enough @Kevin Buzzard but Mathlib also asks for the right proofs, I thought (?), and therein lies the rub ...

I should say that it's more than just compiling and agreed statements. Each PR goes through an AI review process to bring the code up to some standard. But yes making a PR for an existing autoformalisation is one way to do it.

but Mathlib also asks for the right proofs

Yes, but if you have the right definitions and the right statements and the wrong proofs, and you make a PR, then you might quickly find that other people replace them with the right proofs during the review process.

My point is that I think it is feasible - at least with enough people involve - to agree on some number of definitions and statements and then get AI to slop out proofs of these; I don't think it would be fair to try to push those to Mathlib and expect others to write the right proofs. Ok, we have something to think about. We'll take a look at that list!

Yeah I think that the natural way to make progress here is actually to take some example theorems and then ask the usual questions: (1) are all the definitions in place to state them (2) how to state them (3) how to prove them.

Now approximately six weeks ago I started on a project to formalize B. C. Carlson's Special Functions of Applied Mathematics (1977) in Lean. It needed some elementary results from Several Complex Variables (SCV) that were not in Mathlib, and that got me distracted with a project to formalize basic results from that field, and then a further distraction evolved to formalize basic results from single variable complex analysis (CA). The projects are in my GitHub space as lean-SCV and lean-CA. SCV is in the Palomar registry too and I expect CA to wind up there soon. I made very extensive use of multiple LLM as agents and in particular all proofs were done exclusively by LLM. In the overall design I tried to be fully consistent with Mathlib standards; for example, the functions of one or several complex variables have values in a complex Banach space whenever that makes sense.

Thank you again @Snir Broshi . Is the Cauchy integral theorem still not on Mathlib (in a form for general integration paths)? Do you know why - is there a discussion about how general it should be? I feel that this will be quite a roadblock if it isn't resolved. But perhaps I should start a separate thread from the introduction one - probably next week. Thanks again everyone for the comments!!!

Hello @Bastiaan Braams that sounds interesting. Perhaps we should combine our efforts (as well as others interested in formalising complex analysis). My interest is mainly in one variable, but of course it would be good to have several complex variables where results and concepts are general.

Lasse Rempe said:

Is the Cauchy integral theorem still not on Mathlib (in a form for general integration paths)? Do you know why - is there a discussion about how general it should be?

Yes, we still don't know what it says. Do you? The issue is exactly how general the path should be. What would be lovely would be a statement which covers all use cases. Because AFAIK we still don't know what to prove, right now we can't prove the integral of a holomorphic function around a triangle is zero (we can do rectangles and circles though).
There has been plenty of discussion about this on Zulip. Perhaps the search function will already tell you, otherwise I can also take a look later today.

Lasse Rempe said:

Is the Cauchy integral theorem still not on Mathlib (in a form for general integration paths)?

We have docs#DiffContOnCl.circleIntegral_eq_zero for circles, and docs#Complex.integral_boundary_rect_eq_zero_of_differentiableOn for rectangles, and #26479 for unbounded rectangles, but nothing for any simple closed contours.

Kevin Buzzard said:

The issue is exactly how general the path should be.

I think {γ : Path z z} (hinj : Set.InjOn γ {0}ᶜ) (hsub : Set.range γ ⊆ D) (hcon : IsSimplyConnected D) is fine, no?
(plus some differentiability hypothesis)

Lasse Rempe said:

Is the Cauchy integral theorem still not on Mathlib (in a form for general integration paths)? Do you know why - is there a discussion about how general it should be?

Yes, we still don't know what it says. Do you? The issue is exactly how general the path should be. What would be lovely would be a statement which covers all use cases. Because AFAIK we still don't know what to prove, right now we can't prove the integral of a holomorphic function around a triangle is zero (we can do rectangles and circles though).

Well, probably I don't - but perhaps picking something that is sufficiently general to make progress would actually not be such a bad idea? If you put me on the spot, I would say that null-homotopic rectifiable cycles would be more than general enough for most applications. I am sure one can argue about what exactly one should put, but if this is a long-running discussion, perhaps this is a moment to be practical and decide on a good formulation that will be enough to let complex analysis development proceed further? I would leave it to those who have been involved in these discussions before to propose a precise statement, BUT I'd advocate settling on one. :)

Mathlib likes to get it right the first time. I agree that making a reasonable choice would accelerate progress, but the goals of mathlib are not necessarily to accelerate things, the goal is to get it right.

We already have a notion of integral along a curve, as docs#curveIntegral. We could already state the Cauchy integral formula using this integral along a curve with matching endpoints, assuming that the curve is absolutely continuous, say. (One would just need to define the winding number, but this can be done by hand, by lifting the angle along the curve)

What would be nicer, though, is first to extend the notion of curve integral to continuous curves, assuming that the one-form is closed. The definition would be the limit of the curve integral along polygonal approximations, and would be shown not to depend on the chosen approximation, and to give back the curve integral when the curve is absolutely continuous (and ae differentiable if the target space is not finite-dimensional, as this is not automatic then). Then the Cauchy integral formula would still hold for this extended notion of curve integral.
I think @Yury G. Kudryashov had plans to implement all this, but I don't know how it turned out.

The consensus was that working with piecewise C^1 would probably be a worse choice than absolutely continuous, because the definition is in fact more messy. But we would definitely need a theorem saying what the curve integral is in the piecewise C^1 case.

My take on integration of a closed 1-form along a curve is at #PR reviews > #22782 Etale space @ 💬:

Another application of this would be the development of a satisfactory theory of integration of a closed 1-form along any continuous path: this would be defined as the monodromy (#22771) of the covering space in the previous paragraph. The way it is defined, it's automatically
(1) invariant under any continuous deformation (HomotopyRel) of the path/contour and respects concatenation and reversal of paths;
(2) given any primitive f of the 1-form on a domain containing the path, the integral equals the difference of the values of f at the start point and the end point. And it then follows
(3) if the path γ\gammaγ is C1C^1C1, the integral can be computed as ∫01f(γ(t))γ′(t) dt\int_0^1 f(\gamma(t))\gamma'(t)\,dt∫01​f(γ(t))γ′(t)dt: this is easy to prove if there's a primitive FFF of fff in a neighborhood of the path, since F(γ(⋅))F(\gamma(\cdot))F(γ(⋅)) is then a primitive of f(γ(⋅))γ′(⋅)f(\gamma(\cdot))\gamma'(\cdot)f(γ(⋅))γ′(⋅); in general we can subdivide the path so that each piece is contained in a disk, and use additivity from (1).

My original PR #31925 might be a bit too complicated to review, but Yury's #39630 has since landed in Mathlib and seems to be aiming at the same goal (Cauchy integral theorem) ...

Hi all,

I was in Yury's group at the ICERM Analysis workshop this May. We more or less settled on an approach to formalizing the Cauchy integral theorem, using espaces étalés to prove existence of primitives of holomorphic functions on simply connected subsets.

I have a complete Lean proof which is about half human-written and half AI-generated. The AI part was heavily guided, so it is not really AI slop, but it is also not quite mathlib quality yet.

The main advantage of the approach is that it can use the covering-space lifting theorem (IsCoveringMapOn.existsUnique_continuousMap_lifts) to do a substantial part of the work. It also produces a few natural sheaves along the way.

The complex-analytic statement is

theorem exists_global_primitive_of_holomorphic
    {U : Set ℂ} [LocPathConnectedSpace U]
    (f : ℂ → ℂ)
    (hf : DifferentiableOn ℂ f U)
    (hU_open : IsOpen U)
    (hU_sc : IsSimplyConnected U) :
    ∃ G : ℂ → ℂ, ∀ z : ℂ, z ∈ U → HasDerivAt G (f z) z

and more generally we prove

theorem exists_global_primitive_of_closedOn
  {E : Type} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [NormedSpace ℝ E]
  {F : Type} [NormedAddCommGroup F] [NormedSpace ℝ F] [CompleteSpace F]
  {U : Set E} [SimplyConnectedSpace U] [LocPathConnectedSpace U]
  (hU_open : IsOpen U)
  (ω : E → E →L[ℝ] F)
  (hω : DifferentiableOn ℝ ω U)
  (hω_symm : ∀ a ∈ U, ∀ x y, (fderiv ℝ ω a x) y = (fderiv ℝ ω a y) x) :
    ∃ G : E → F, ∀ z : E, z ∈ U → HasFDerivAt G (ω z) z

I had planned to clean this up and PR it (I was building on Yury's PR), but never quite got around to it. I was unaware of PR #31925 and I think there could be a substantial overlap.

I also have a final-year undergraduate student who was supposed to push this over the finish line and PR it. But he could also work on the residue theorem, which was my original goal, and I could try to PR it soon.

I am also rather new to all things Lean, so If anyone has suggestions for how best to proceed, I would be very grateful. I have also been somewhat absent from Zulip, so I do not know whether more related work exists already.

Hello @Lars Kuehne I know nothing about Étale spaces, but I think it would be great to have the Cauchy integral theorem in Lean one way or another. What needs to happen before you can create a pull request?

I think an important distinction between my approach at #31925 and @Yury Kudryashov (Harmonic)'s approach is that I start from an arbitrary family of types and define topology on the Sigma type given a predicate on sections, while Yury specializes to the family of germs of a presheaf. I think my setup is a natural middle ground between sheaves and spaces ((Pre)localPredicates gives rise to (pre)sheaves and is used to define sheafification), and is also more convenient for the application to primitives of a holomorphic function (or closed 1-form). In this case we have a constant family of types (ℂ) over some domain in the complex plane, and the condition of being a primitive on an open subset is a local predicate. You can take the associated sheaf and then its germs and they are naturally identified with ℂ, but not defeq, and working with ℂ directly is of course more convenient than the germs. So I think the best way going forward is still to get #31925 into Mathlib.

Monodromy of the etale space associated to a closed 1-form on a differentiable manifold could be used to define the pairing between the 1st de Rham cohomology and the 1st singular homology (or rather the abelianization of the fundamental group in our treatment). For the version of the residue theorem at #maths > Multivariate complex analysis @ 💬, we'll need to show that every closed curve in a simply connected domain minus a finite number of points is homologic to small loops around those points with multiplicities given by winding numbers. This needs to use either Van Kampen (someone needs to clean up or rewrite #41603) or Mayer-Vietoris (exists in TauCeti but not Mathlib IIRC). These along with API for integration along continuous paths I mentioned earlier are what should be established if the goal is to contribute the residue theorem to Mathlib, in my opinion.

Some more details. We have an action of ℂ on the etale space by translation on each fiber, which makes the projection docs#IsAddQuotientCoveringMap. docs#IsAddQuotientCoveringMap.fundamentalGroupToMulOpposite then gives a map from the fundamental group to ℂ which defines integration along a based loop. Since ℂ is abelian this factors through the abelianization, which is the 1st singular homology group.

In the setup of the residue theorem, the base of the etale space is a simply connected domain with a finitely many (or a (necessarily countable) closed discrete set of) punctures, and we need to show that if a loop has zero winding number around each puncture then it is trivial in the abelianization. The simply connected domain is the union of the punctured domain with a small disc around each puncture, so by Van Kampen, its (trivial) fundamental groupoid can be obtained from that of the punctured domain by killing a small loop around each puncture, which means that the fundamental group of the punctured domain is normally generated by those small loops (conjugated by some path from the base point to the small loops). Each small loop has winding number 1 around one puncture and 0 around other punctures, so in any word representing a loop with zero winding number around a puncture, the corresponding small loop appears with net multiplicity 0, so it can be eliminated in the abelianization; if this happens for every puncture then the loop is trivial in the abelianization. Winding number on the plane hasn't been defined in Mathlib but should be analogous to docs#AddCircle.windingNumber.

If you want to show that the fundamental group is actually freely generated by the small loops, the easiest way I can think of is to use the Riemann mapping theorem to show that the simply connected domain is homeomorphic to ℂ, order the punctures by (modulus, argument), construct a self-homeomorphism of ℂ that sends the punctures to ℕ ⊆ ℂ, and use Van Kampen with the open cover by {z | n - 1 < Re z < n + 1} and {z | Re z < 0} to compute the fundamental group of ℂ \ ℕ.

I hope people get to work on these during #Event announcements > Sphere Packing "Packathon" at EPFL: November 2026, which I am unfortunately unable to attend.

It's probably appropriate to move discussions starting from #new members > Introducing myself: Lasse Rempe @ 💬 to some "path integral / residue theorem" thread under #maths, but I'm unable to move messages across channels.
